# Genesis 12 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Genesis 12 is described as the "watershed chapter of the entire Bible" — a turning point from God dealing with humanity en masse (Genesis 1–11) to God choosing one man and one nation through whom redemption would come (Genesis 12–50). Precept Austin notes that some professors consider the division between Genesis 11 and 12 "greater in importance than the division between the Old and New Testaments."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-12-commentary

---

## v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Abram, 'Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you.'"

**Traditional Reading:**

- **The call came originally in Ur.** Stephen's speech in Acts 7:2–4 reveals God first spoke to Abram while still in Mesopotamia, before the family moved to Haran. Genesis 12:1–3 repeats the promise after Terah's death, when Abram was called to more complete obedience. (Guzik, Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **Two calls.** Gill explains there were likely two divine appearances: one in Ur and a second in Haran after Terah died. The second call is marked by the added phrase "and from your father's house," which Stephen omits when citing the first call (Acts 7:3), because at the first call Terah and the family came with Abram. At the second, Terah was dead and Nahor's family stayed behind. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **"Get thee out" = separation.** God called Abram out of an idolatrous environment. Gill notes the Zabaeans (as Maimonides called them) worshipped sun, moon, and stars; Abram was raised among them but dissented. The Hebrew literally reads "go to thee" — for thy profit and good (Jarchi). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **"Kindred" = birthplace?** Ellicott argues the Hebrew word more probably means "thy birthplace" (as in Gen 11:28), settling that the command came at Ur rather than Haran. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **The land not named.** Both Gill and Ellicott note that Canaan was deliberately not mentioned at first, to test Abram's faith — hence Hebrews 11:8 says "he went out, not knowing whither he went." The knowledge of Canaan as the destination may have come only later. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **NT application.** Precept Austin and Spurgeon both stress that Abram's call is a picture of the believer's effectual calling — "come out from among them, and be ye separate" (2 Cor 6:17). Abram's call represents being separated from the world by omnipotent grace. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-12-commentary ; https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/effectual-calling-illustrated-by-the-call-of-abram

---

## v. 2 — "I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"I will" — the promise rests on God, not Abram.** Guzik emphasises that God repeats "I will" many times in these verses. Genesis 11 is about the plans of man; Genesis 12 is all about the plans of God. God's promise is more important than Abram's faith. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **"Be thou a blessing."** Ellicott notes the Hebrew is an imperative — "Be thou a blessing" — not a prediction ("thou shalt be"). This marks "a higher level": Abram's faith is not to be selfish. In return for becoming a stranger, he is to procure religious privileges for all families of the earth. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Spiritual and literal nation.** Gill explains "great nation" in two senses: literally the Jewish people descended from Abram, and spiritually all believers in all ages who walk in the steps of Abram's faith (Gal 3:7). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **"I will bless thee" = principally spiritual.** Gill lists adoption, justification by imputed righteousness, faith, sanctification, and eternal glory — since Abram personally never possessed the land of Canaan. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **"Make thy name great."** Abram is honoured by Jews, Muslims, and Christians — "probably no more honoured name in history." Gill adds that his name is also famous in profane (secular) history. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **"Be a blessing" = either a blessing to others or "blessing itself."** Gill offers both interpretations: Abram would be a channel of spiritual blessing to others, or the phrase intensively means "exceedingly blessed." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

---

## v. 3 — "I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Two different Hebrew verbs for "curse."** Ellicott points out an essential distinction: the first verb ("curse" in "curse those who curse you") means "to treat lightly, revile, or speak contemptuously of"; the second means "to pronounce a judicial curse." The sense is: "I will pass a sentence of rejection upon him that revileth thee." These verbs appear together in Exodus 22:28, rendered "revile" and "curse." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **"Shall be blessed," not "shall bless themselves."** Ellicott notes some translate the Hebrew reflexively ("shall bless themselves"), but there is a different conjugation for that meaning and no reason to force it here. The text means that through Abram, blessing will actively come to all families. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Fulfilled in Christ.** Guzik and Gill both identify this as the great Messianic promise: "in thee" means "in thy seed" (Gen 22:18), interpreted of Christ in Acts 3:25 and Galatians 3:8. Not every individual, but as many as believe in Christ of all nations are blessed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **The second major Messianic prophecy.** Precept Austin notes Genesis 3:15 is the first, Genesis 12:1–3 is the second, and Genesis 49:10 ("until Shiloh comes") is the third major Messianic prediction in Genesis. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-12-commentary

- **"All families of the earth" = the adâmâh.** Ellicott notes this refers not to the material universe but to the ground in its connection with man — wherever man makes his home, through Abram spiritual blessings will be offered. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **"Bless those who bless you" — a principle that remains.** Guzik says this promise, inherited by the covenant descendants of Abram (the Jewish people), remains true today and "is a root reason for the decline and death of many empires." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

---

## v. 4 — "So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Partial obedience: Lot.** Guzik observes that God commanded Abram to leave his "family" (v.1), yet he brought his nephew Lot. This partial obedience "would later bring nothing but trouble." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **Abram's age and Terah's chronology.** Gill explains mathematically: Terah died at 205 (Gen 11:32); Abram was 75 at departure; therefore Abram was born when Terah was 130, not 70. This means Abram was not Terah's eldest son (though listed first in Gen 11:26 as the most important). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **Immediate obedience.** Gill notes that "as soon as ever the words were spoken … he immediately prepared and got all things ready." Cocceius renders it "when the Lord had spoken to him" — his obedience was instantaneous. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

**Reformed / Baptist emphasis (Spurgeon):**

- Spurgeon calls Abram's obedience "an act of heroic faith" — those Eastern people "trembled even to cross the Euphrates or the Tigris" and considered a journey of two or three hundred miles "an event only second to death itself." — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/abrahams-double-blessing

- Spurgeon also preached that the call is "often only half obeyed" — Terah and family set out from Ur toward Canaan but stopped at Haran (Gen 11:31). Half-way obedience is not enough. — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/abrams-call-or-half-way-and-all-the-way

---

## v. 5 — "And Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all the possessions and people they had acquired in Haran, and set out for the land of Canaan."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"The souls that they had gotten"** — Ellicott notes the Hebrew literally says "had made." Onkelos and Jewish interpreters explain this as **proselytes**: persons Abram and Sarai had converted to faith in the one God. However, most were probably dependents and slaves. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Gill confirms:** the Chaldee paraphrases (Targums) say "the souls which they made subject to the law in Haran" and "the souls of the proselytes." Jarchi adds: "Abram proselyted the men, and Sarai the women." However, the literal sense includes servants bought with money — both categories together formed the 318 trained servants of Gen 14:14. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **"Into the land of Canaan they came"** — Gill says this clause is "very fitly added" because previously, when they left Ur, they "went forth to go into the land of Canaan" (Gen 11:31) but stopped at Haran. This time they completed the journey — about 300 miles. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **Abram as "the Hebrew"** — Ellicott connects this to the crossing (passing over) of the Euphrates, probably at the ford at Carchemish (Jerabolus). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

---

## v. 6 — "Abram traveled through the land as far as the site of the Oak of Moreh at Shechem. And at that time the Canaanites were in the land."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Not "plain" but "oak."** Ellicott corrects the translation: the Hebrew is "the oak of Moreh" (êlôn), not "plain." It was probably a grove of oaks (the quercus pseudococcifera). "Moreh" literally means "teacher" (Isaiah 9:15) — possibly a place where a religious teacher once instructed the people. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Shechem = "shoulder."** The name describes the ridge uniting Mounts Ebal and Gerizim. The modern name is Nablous (from Flavia Neapolis, named in honour of Vespasian). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **"The Canaanite was then in the land"** — Ellicott insists this is **not** a sign of post-Mosaic authorship (as if they were there "then" but not later). Rather, it means Abram found the land already occupied by Canaanites, even though it had originally belonged to Semitic stock. This was a **test of Abram's faith**: the land promised to his seed was already inhabited. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

---

## v. 7 — "Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, 'I will give this land to your offspring.' So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **First divine "appearance" in Scripture.** Ellicott marks this as significant: previously God's communications had been direct, without visible medium (God "said" to Adam, Cain, Noah). Now we read repeatedly of a visible manifestation, later connected with the "Angel of Jehovah." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **The appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ?** Both Ellicott (who discusses whether this was a created angel or an anticipation of the incarnation) and Gill (who says "it was the Son of God") raise the question. Gill states: "whenever there was any visible appearance of a divine Person, under the former dispensation, it seems to be always of the essential Word, that was to be incarnate." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **The land promise narrowed.** For the first time God specifically says He will **give** the land (not just "show" it, as in v. 1). Guzik notes that Abram saw the land with his physical eyes. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **Altar = taking possession.** By building an altar, Abram "took possession of the land for Jehovah, and consecrated it to Him." It was also a place of public worship and sacrifice — parallel to Noah's altar (Gen 8:20). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

---

## v. 8 — "From there Abram moved on to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. There he built an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Nomad life.** Ellicott says "he removed" means he broke up his encampment — the usual nomad pattern. His wealth in cattle would make frequent moves necessary. The hill country between Bethel and Ai was fertile in antiquity (almond trees, aqueducts), though now "uninviting." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Bethel = "house of God."** This name was given later by Jacob (Gen 28:19); before Abram's time the place was called Luz. Moses uses the later name by anticipation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **"Called on the name of the LORD"** — Gill explains this as prayer for fresh mercies and thanksgiving for past ones. He adds an important theological note: "he called upon Jehovah the Father, in the name of his Son, the glorious Mediator, who had appeared unto him, and whose day he saw and was glad." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **Tent = sojourner.** Gill notes the tent "fitly represents the state of the people of God, as sojourners in this world … having no abiding place." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **Worship pattern.** Both at Shechem and Bethel, Abram built altars and worshipped publicly — "wherever he went he worshipped God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

---

## v. 9 — "And Abram journeyed on toward the Negev."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **The Negev = the dry land.** Ellicott explains the name comes from the soft white chalk soil through which rains sink. Though treeless, it was rich in flocks and herds, with water collected in tanks and cisterns. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Moving south toward Egypt.** Gill notes that this movement southward brought Abram nearer to Egypt, setting up the next section. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **John Phillips (Precept Austin) titles this section "Forsaking the Path of Faith"** — suggesting Abram's southward drift was the beginning of his movement away from the place of God's promise. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-12-commentary

---

## v. 10 — "Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while, because the famine was severe."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **A test of faith.** Guzik says a famine was a serious problem — many died — and it was right for Abram to be concerned. But he was wrong in thinking God would not provide in the place where God called him. "Abram found it easier to trust God in far-off promises than in right-now needs." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **Timing.** Ellicott calculates the famine occurred within about eight years of Abram's arrival in Canaan (based on Abram being 75 at departure, and Ishmael being born when Abram was 86 — Gen 16:16). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Faith shown in "sojourn."** Ellicott notes Abram went to Egypt only "to sojourn" — not to settle. This shows he intended to return to Canaan, which "is a proof of Abram's faith." He neither retraced his steps toward Haran (Hebrews 11:15) nor sought a new permanent home. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Egypt vs. Canaan.** Gill notes the contrast: Egypt was south-west; Chaldea (home) was north-east. Abram went in the opposite direction from home, showing he would not go back. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm

- **Why Egypt?** Egypt was watered by the Nile's flooding caused by Abyssinian rains, so a local failure in South Palestine would not affect Egypt. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

---

## vv. 11–13 — Abram's scheme: "Please say you are my sister"

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Sarai's age and beauty.** Though 65 years old, Sarai retained much of her early beauty. Ellicott suggests her light (fair) complexion would especially commend her to the "swarthy descendants of Ham," who were "not a handsome race, but had flat foreheads, high cheek-bones, large mouths, and thick lips." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **A half-truth was a whole lie.** Guzik notes Sarai was indeed Abram's half-sister (Gen 20:12), so the statement was technically a half-truth. But the intent was to deceive, and Abram "trusted in his deception to protect him instead of trusting in the Lord." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **A pre-arranged scheme.** Ellicott points out from Genesis 20:13 that this was not a spur-of-the-moment plan — Abram and Sarai had agreed on it when they first left Haran. This "mixture of faith and weakness, of trust in God in abandoning so much and trust in worldly policy for preservation in a foreseen danger," reveals "how much of infirmity there was even in a character otherwise so noble." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **"That it may be well with me for thy sake."** Abram's primary stated concern was his own safety ("they will kill me but let you live"), not Sarai's welfare. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

---

## vv. 14–16 — Sarai taken into Pharaoh's house; Abram prospers

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Pharaoh = a title, not a name.** Ellicott explains the derivation: per-ao or phar-ao means "the double house" or "palace" — a title veiling the monarch under the name of his dwelling, like "the Court." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **"Princes" = border officials.** Ellicott suggests these were commanders at the frontier fortresses built by Pharaoh Amenemhai to control Semitic immigration. At the wall, a powerful sheik like Abram would be interrogated and a report sent to Pharaoh. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Women went unveiled in Egypt** until the Persian conquest, so the officials had full opportunity to observe Sarai's unusual lightness of complexion. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **The gifts.** Ellicott notes it was customary to give a sum of money when taking a daughter or sister to wife. The largeness of the presents proves Pharaoh believed he was acting lawfully. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **God blessed Abram anyway.** Guzik notes: "God blessed Abram even when he didn't trust and obey God as he should." The promise depended on God, not on Abram. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

---

## v. 17 — "The LORD, however, afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram's wife Sarai."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Timing of the plagues.** Ellicott suggests the plagues occurred during the interval before the marriage could take place. Citing Esther 2:12 (twelve months of preparation for maidens), he posits "Sarai was probably saved by some such formality." During this waiting period, Pharaoh and his household experienced "such marked troubles that he became alarmed." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Divine protection.** Guzik emphasises: God's protection of Sarai shows that if Abram had trusted God and told the truth, "everything would have been all right." God was faithful even when Abram was faithless. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

---

## vv. 18–20 — Pharaoh rebukes Abram

**Traditional Reading:**

- **A pagan king rebukes the man of faith.** Guzik highlights the irony: "Sadly, a pagan king had to rebuke Abram." Pharaoh's conduct is "upright and dignified." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **"What have you done to me?"** Ellicott notes that Pharaoh's indignation is just. He says "I took her with the intention of making her my wife" — the Hebrew reads "and I took her to me to wife," meaning the marriage had not yet been consummated. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Abram's silence.** Ellicott observes: "The silence of Abram seems to indicate his consciousness that Pharaoh had acted more righteously than himself." Yet Abram later repeated the same offence (Genesis 20), showing he "did not feel much self-reproach." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

- **Pharaoh "sent them away."** Ellicott says Pharaoh gave orders that Abram and all his possessions be escorted out — Pharaoh "gave his men orders concerning Abram" (v.20), probably providing safe passage. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**What I could find:**

- **Reformed (John Piper / Desiring God):** Emphasises God's **sovereign grace** in choosing Abram — "an undeserving idolater" (Joshua 24:2) — and that the covenant promises ultimately belong to all who are "children of Abraham through faith in Christ" (Gal 3:29). The blessing is not for Abraham's ethnic descendants alone but for all nations. Piper also structures the promises into three groups: (1) posterity and land, (2) justification by faith (Gen 15:6), (3) blessing to all families of the earth. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-covenant-of-abraham

- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Stresses **effectual calling, separation, and obedience.** Abram's call is a picture of how God sovereignly calls sinners out of the world. Spurgeon repeatedly emphasises that "half-way" obedience (like stopping at Haran) is disobedience. He also focuses on the believer's separated life — not monastic withdrawal, but living in the world with "a higher tone of morals … a life with God." — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/abrahams-double-blessing ; https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/abrams-call-or-half-way-and-all-the-way

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (David Guzik / Enduring Word):** Emphasises the **ongoing validity of the promise** that God blesses those who bless Israel (v.3) and links it to the rise and fall of empires. Guzik also stresses God's **grace covering Abram's failures** — the promise depended on God, not Abram's performance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-12/

- **Older Baptist/Anglican (Gill, Ellicott):** Gill consistently interprets the promises Christologically and sees in the text a picture of the **gospel call** — "an emblem of the call of men by the grace of God out of the world." Ellicott provides the careful philological detail (the two different verbs for "curse," the debate over "bless themselves" vs. "be blessed") and historical context that has influenced all subsequent traditions. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/12.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/12.htm

**What I could not find (search limits):** Distinctively Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), MacArthur's Baptist perspective (gty.org), and Catholic/Orthodox readings were inaccessible due to search limits being reached. I also could not locate NET Bible translation notes or bibleodyssey.org modern scholarship. I was unable to find sources representing prosperity/word of faith interpretations from any of the approved sites — this is likely because the approved sites are largely cessationist or Reformed-leaning and do not host prosperity-gospel teaching.

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across All Sources

1. **Genesis 12 is the great turning point** — from God dealing with all humanity (Gen 1–11) to God's redemptive plan through one man and one nation.
2. **The promise depends on God, not Abram** — the repeated "I will" statements show divine sovereignty.
3. **The call involves separation** — from country, kindred, and father's house — a pattern for every believer's effectual calling.
4. **The promise is ultimately fulfilled in Christ** — "all the families of the earth" are blessed through Abram's Seed (Gal 3:16).
5. **Abram's faith was real but imperfect** — partial obedience (bringing Lot), fear-driven deception in Egypt, yet God remained faithful.
6. **God's grace covers failure** — Abram prospered even in Egypt, yet also suffered consequences (rebuke from a pagan king, "excess baggage").
